decisions.text: Extraction runs behind an evidence gate that prefers under-claiming: each decision, action and risk links to its source in the recording.

decisions.title: Release gates

details.flow_title: How an instruction becomes a working build

flow.name: Ask
flow.detail: An instruction in plain language, such as “add Retrofit and sync the project”

flow.detail: The planner reads the project and picks the tools and their order

flow.name: Act
flow.detail: The executor drives the IDE: read and edit files, add dependencies, sync Gradle, run the app

flow.name: Check
flow.detail: A critic reviews each result; a failed build goes back to the planner with its log

details.rail: The IDE, Gradle and the agent run on the same phone. The model is Gemini through its API, or a Llama model loaded on demand from the app’s assets.

specs: plugin architecture, AI, critical bugs, performance

decisions.title: A critic before the developer
decisions.text: A second model checks every tool result, and a failed build goes back to the planner with its log. On a small screen, each round trip the agent fixes on its own is one less context switch for the developer.

decisions.title: A model that runs on the phone
decisions.text: A Llama model runs on the device. It loads on demand from the app’s assets, so the base install stays small, and requests wait in a queue while the inference engine starts.

decisions.title: AI as plugins
decisions.text: I moved the AI features out of the app into plugins, with contracts for agent tools, LLM inference, embeddings and prompt templates, so new models and tools ship without changing the IDE.

decisions.title: Limits on the agent
decisions.text: Sub-agents can no longer loop forever, chat sessions save safely when the agent’s folder is missing, and the agent reads the real build log instead of a summary.

mobile.title: Native iOS and Android
mobile.text: Native apps for banking and trust products, a security-focused app, a health app, a high-volume restaurant ordering app, a Web3 wallet and an online art marketplace with augmented reality. It started in 2015 with an accessible learning platform for blind and visually impaired students.

highlights.text: Designed the architecture and built the platform end to end with a small team and Claude Code agents: backend, web app, Chrome extension, iOS companion app and infrastructure.
Built chunked, checkpointed Google Gemini transcription with speaker detection, and extraction of decisions, actions and risks with source links behind an evidence gate that prefers under-claiming.
Built Python/FastAPI services and Celery queues with workers across two hosts, backed by MySQL, Redis and ChromaDB vector search, with LangGraph and an MCP server for AI assistants.

Built the Google Cloud infrastructure as code with Terraform (Dec 2025 – Mar 2026): 20 reusable modules across preprod and prod for Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks, Cloud Scheduler, KMS, Secret Manager, IAM, VPC, HTTPS load balancing, Cloud CDN, Artifact Registry and Cloud Storage.
Operated blue/green Docker deployments through Jenkins with host-health admission, deploy locks and exact-commit authorization; images are built on remote compute nodes and pulled by digest.
Review AI coding agents’ code, designs and incident write-ups every day with detailed written feedback, and gate merges and releases on passing tests and production evidence.

Built the iOS companion app in Swift and SwiftUI: AVFoundation microphone capture, ReplayKit broadcast capture and AVKit playback; async/await with actor-isolated resumable uploads, persisted upload manifests, device-flow sign-in, Keychain storage, App Intents and unit tests.
Built a Manifest V3 Chrome extension in JavaScript that records Google Meet, Teams and Zoom, streams live audio and video chunks, signs in through device flow and retries uploads.
Built the web app with Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind, tested with Vitest and Playwright, with PostHog analytics.
Built isolated cloud-browser rooms streamed over WebRTC to run and record meetings, with per-room operators, a microphone guard and per-meeting attendance measurement.
Implemented server-side recovery of interrupted live recordings by reassembling streamed WebM segments, including segments missing their header, and reprocessing the recovered audio automatically.
Added a voice-presence gate so silent screen recordings receive structured visual summaries (timestamped steps, on-screen text and results) instead of hallucinated transcripts.

Built the multi-tenant product in English and Spanish with Jira, GitHub, Slack, calendar and MCP integrations, tenant-scoped view, edit, send and admin permissions, personal access tokens and consent capture.

Built live-meeting Slack status and remote controls to mute the microphone, turn off the camera and leave calls, with channel-wide authorization, audit trails and automatic post-meeting summary checks.
Built per-person daily status that reconciles Jira, Azure DevOps, Notion, Plane and GitHub data with Slack and meeting evidence.
Implemented zero-downtime deployments, traffic splitting, rollback scripts, Cloud Run health probes and a scale-to-zero office-hours mode to reduce idle cost.
Added Prometheus and Grafana alerting, Sentry/GlitchTip crash triage with deduplicated GlitchTip-to-Jira automation, and OpenBao (Vault-compatible) secrets management.

items.title: Code on the Go, an open-source Android IDE that runs on the phone
items.context: App Dev for All (nonprofit), full-time, remote

highlights.text: Built the IDE’s AI agent: a planner, an executor that drives the IDE’s own tools (files, dependencies, Gradle sync, build and run) and a critic that sends failed builds back with their logs.
Designed a modular AI Core plugin that routes between on-device GGUF models (llama.cpp), Google Gemini and OpenAI, with MCP tools, inline code suggestions, vector search and speech-to-text.
Helped bring offline Llama inference into the agent, loaded on demand from the app’s assets, and fixed memory leaks on low-end phones.
Moved the AI features into plugins and designed the plugin API’s contracts for agent tools, LLM inference, embeddings, prompt templates and quick builds.
Took over the on-device Sketch to UI module (YOLOv8) and shipped it as its own plugin: a hand-drawn screen becomes an Android layout, with OCR clean-up, a UI grammar and widget attribute parsing.
Fixed crashes, ANRs and threading bugs found on real phones, and adapted the editor and navigation to large screens, mouse and keyboard.
Wrote the project’s article on the Gemini agent for the App Dev for All blog (March 2026) and the tablet wiki.
Migrated legacy Android XML layouts to Jetpack Compose with ViewModel/MVVM patterns for maintainable state and UI behavior.
Built and maintained native and cross-platform features across iOS and Android: Swift native modules, Kotlin, Flutter, and React Native features with native bridges.
Used Flutter with Dart, flutter_bloc and the Singular SDK for predictable state management, attribution and analytics.
Added WidgetKit extension targets and shared code schemes to bring app state to iOS widgets.
Worked on build configuration, dependencies and CI/CD release workflows with GitHub Actions and Tekton for repeatable mobile delivery.
Built the token-swap flow and Android features with Jetpack Compose, Hilt and the repository pattern.
Implemented chat replies and reactions, a fiat on-ramp UI and the Kotlin DSL migration in sprint work with the client’s teams.
Developed and maintained production iOS features in Swift, including augmented-reality art visualization and catalog experiences.
Built and improved AR features with ARKit and SceneKit, with attention to rendering behavior, interaction quality and performance.
Integrated REST API catalog data flows, working with designers, QA and project managers.
Managed beta and production builds, TestFlight delivery and App Store publication with QA and project stakeholders.

items.title: Client engagements for a software consultancy

highlights.text: Built features with native iOS modules in Swift and Android-facing integrations: HealthKit, deep links, push notifications, background delivery and offline-aware serialization.
Used Firebase, Sentry and PostHog for analytics, observability and production visibility across mobile releases.
Developed secure native apps in Swift and Kotlin focused on protected user workflows, fraud-aware flows and reliable communication between the app and its backend.
Integrated secure REST APIs and AWS-backed services with native modules for asynchronous workflows, data integrity and responsive user experiences.
Led Android and iOS initiatives to improve app performance and UX and to coordinate scalable, backend-connected data flows for high-volume consumer use.
Built and maintained Android features in Kotlin with modern native architecture, working with backend teams on analytics, personalization, secure data access and transaction processing.
Took part in the first Flutter experiments for cross-platform delivery, validating shared UI flows, state-management options and native-integration trade-offs.
Delivered secure mobile features for financial products on Android and iOS: Kotlin and Java, iOS support, automated testing, secure transactions and backend-connected workflows.

Designed and developed an inclusive mobile learning platform for blind and visually impaired users with Android (Java/Kotlin), tactile feedback, audio narration, accessibility-first UX and device integration.

hood.title: Under the hood
hood.description: How this site is built: live readings of your visit, what each part weighs, its security policy, and the front-end techniques behind it, each with its code.
hood.lede: This site is its own datasheet. The first readings are your visit, measured by your browser while you read. The rest is how the page is built, what it weighs, and the techniques behind it, each with its code.
hood.live_note: Measured by your browser with the Performance APIs: the same numbers this site’s anonymous metrics collect.

live.inp: Slowest response to a tap or key

hood.interact: tap or press a key to measure
hood.noscript: These readings need JavaScript; everything else on the site works without it.
hood.no: no: the page works without it
hood.build_lede: Plain PHP and hand-written CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no bundler, no runtime dependency, and nothing loaded from another domain.
hood.weights_note: Bytes as served, with gzip. Images and video load only when they come into view, so they are not counted.
hood.csp_note: Scripts and styles only from this site and nothing inline. Every technique below had to work inside it.

techniques.title: Instant case studies
techniques.what: Chrome prerenders a case study as soon as you show intent (hover, or touch on a phone), so the click opens it at once, and the card’s screen and title travel into the new page.
techniques.hard: Speculation rules usually live in an inline script, which this security policy forbids, so they arrive in an HTTP header. The morph spans two documents: each side names its elements as the page leaves and as the next one appears.

techniques.title: A source for every claim
techniques.what: Each claim in the introduction opens the roles behind it, next to its button.
techniques.hard: Opening, closing, Esc and focus come from the Popover API, and the placement from CSS anchor positioning, which only reached every major browser in 2026. No script opens, places or closes it.

techniques.title: The capability chip
techniques.what: The chip tilts toward the pointer, the pins near it light up, and picking one shows where that skill was used.
techniques.hard: One pointer listener, throttled to the frame rate, drives the tilt, the glow and the magnetic buttons. It runs only with a mouse or trackpad and never with reduced motion.

techniques.title: Experience as a scope trace
techniques.what: A signal runs down the Experience list as you read, and each role is a pulse that lights up when it reaches the reading line.
techniques.hard: It is drawn by scroll-driven animations (a view timeline per role, inset so the trace head sits 65% down the screen), in CSS with no script and no scroll listener. Without support, or with reduced motion, the trace is simply drawn.

techniques.title: Circuit traces on the GPU
techniques.what: Picking a pin sends a pulse along a printed-circuit trace from that pin, down beside the chip, into the panel that shows the evidence.
techniques.hard: It is a WebGPU shader: every pixel measures its distance to each trace segment, so lines and glow stay sharp at any pixel density with no geometry to rebuild. The traces are routed like a board, so none cross. The code loads only on the first pick, renders only while the pulse moves, and is skipped with reduced motion or without WebGPU.

techniques.title: The mark calibrates
techniques.what: On the first page of a visit the logo’s middle slice steps into place and its bar is drawn.
techniques.hard: It is CSS on the inline SVG, with no animation library, played once per visit and skipped with reduced motion.

techniques.title: A theme from one colour
techniques.what: Every surface and text colour comes from the logo’s cobalt.
techniques.hard: The tones are generated with Material Color Utilities (HCT) and Material 3 roles, then each text, outline and logo pair is measured against WCAG.

techniques.title: Metrics without cookies
techniques.what: Anonymous counts of what people read and click, with no cookie and no third-party script.
techniques.hard: Events go to this site and the server forwards only an allow-list of fields. A prerendered page holds its events until it is actually shown.

items.title: Where a fake recruiter's malware gets its orders: five contracts on Polygon in 37 seconds
items.description: A take-home test from a fake recruiter reads its server address from a Polygon smart contract. The contract's public history shows one wallet, five identical contracts in 37 seconds, and team labels.
items.author: John Andrés Trujillo

runs.s: In October a "recruiter" sent me a coding test for a crypto project. I didn't run it on my laptop. I took it apart in an isolated lab instead, and found that it doesn't carry its server address. It asks a smart contract on Polygon for it, a technique
Google's threat intelligence team calls EtherHiding
This week Binance said the same play, a fake interview with a take-home repo,
. So I went back to my sample. A contract is public by design, which means its whole history is public too. This is what that history shows.

items.s: The sample asks a Polygon contract for its server with a read-only call that is free and leaves no transaction.
One wallet funded five new wallets, and they deployed five byte-identical contracts within 37 seconds, each labeled with a team number.
The contract my sample reads changed servers once, on 18 September, and has pointed at the same address since.
Anyone can read that history, defenders included: every server change is a permanent, timestamped record.
Take-home code is untrusted code. Run it in a throwaway VM, never on the laptop you work from.

body.text: How the sample finds its server

runs.s: Instead of a hard-coded domain, the loader calls
on a contract through a Polygon RPC endpoint. The key is a short ASCII string packed into a
: read-only, free, and not a transaction, so the infected machines leave nothing on the chain when they ask.
To move every infected machine to a new server, the owner sends one
transaction. There is no domain to seize and no DNS record to sinkhole.

Polygon stores bytecode, not source code. I hashed candidate function signatures with keccak-256 and matched them against the selectors in the bytecode to recover the interface. The event name came out the same way, from its topic hash. Here is a reconstruction that behaves the same. It is not the attackers' source:

items.s: Only the owner can write.
There is a
transferOwnership
, but no
renounceOwnership
and no way to self-destruct, so the contract cannot be deleted. The owner can re-point it at any time.
Every write is labeled.
Each update sets the key the malware uses and, right after it, a readable key such as
team2
with the same URL.

caption.s: One funding wallet, five fresh wallets, five byte-identical contracts. The sample I received reads team2.

runs.s: The wallet that deployed my sample's contract had a nonce of 0 at the time: it was brand new. Polygon emits a fee-transfer log for every transaction, so filtering those logs by address lists a wallet's transactions without an indexer. That led to the wallet that funded it, and to its siblings:

items.s: one wallet sends 0.9 POL to each of five new wallets.
each of the five deploys the same bytecode, about one every 9 seconds.
Minutes later:
each contract gets a server URL and a label: team1, team2, team3, team9, team10. Mine is team2.

runs.s: The numbering has gaps, with no team4 to team8 from this funder. That suggests more groups than these five. I didn't search other funders.
as of any past block. These are the values for my sample's key on
, by date. I've masked part of each server address:
The other teams moved more. Team3 changed servers three times in its first eleven days, and team1 moved on 20 October. On 3 November, the day
The Hacker News published Binance's findings
, team9 was re-pointed to a server my sample already used for its keylogger and clipboard agents. That is a timing coincidence. Nothing here shows a cause.

For the operators, a contract is infrastructure that survives takedowns: no hosting account to close, no domain to seize, and reads that cost nothing. For defenders, the same property is a gift. The contract is a public log of every server change, with a block number and a timestamp, and nobody can edit it after the fact.
Blocking public RPC endpoints isn't practical for most teams. Watching for
events on known contracts is, and so is alerting when a developer machine makes
requests it has no reason to make.

items.s: Treat a take-home repo like an attachment from a stranger. Open it in a throwaway VM with no SSH keys, no wallet, no cloud credentials and no logged-in browser.
Read the install and build scripts before you install anything. That is where a loader can hide.
If a "recruiter" pushes you to run it today, on your own machine, the urgency is the tell.

Method: passive reads only, through public Polygon RPC endpoints. I never used the RPC endpoint configured in the sample and never contacted the servers it points to.

items.title: A coding agent on the phone it builds for: lessons from Code on the Go
items.description: What it took to run an AI coding agent inside Code on the Go, an offline Android IDE on the phone: RAM-sized local models, safe tool calls, approvals.
items.author: John Andrés Trujillo

runs.s: is an open-source Android IDE that runs on the phone itself, without a laptop and without Internet access. I built its AI agent: you ask in plain language, and it reads, edits, builds and fixes your project on the device. In March I described what the agent does
on the App Dev for All blog

. This post is about what it took underneath, because calling a model was never the hard part. The hard part is that the phone running the agent is also running the IDE, Gradle and the app being built, all from the same RAM. And a user who picks a local model expects their code to stay on that phone.

items.s: I built the AI agent for Code on the Go — an open-source Android IDE that runs, and runs an LLM, entirely on the phone, offline.
The hard part isn't calling a model; it's that the model shares the phone's RAM with the IDE, Gradle and the app being built.
Local models are sized to the RAM that's free at that moment, kept on-device by permission, and constrained by a grammar so a small model can't emit a broken tool call.
An agent is only as good as the evidence you feed it: real build output, not its own word — and every change is gated behind approval.

body.text: One router, and no model of its own

runs.s: The agent started inside the app in September 2025. It talked to Gemini through the Firebase AI SDK, behind a repository that switched between Gemini and a local Llama engine. By July 2026 I had moved the AI features into plugins: about 50 classes, the llama.cpp native libraries and the bundled AAR left the main app, and the plugin API grew what the agent needed, with additive changes only, so existing plugins kept loading.

caption.s: AI Core is a router. Consumers on the left call it; it routes to whichever backend the user selected on the right.

runs.s: Today the AI Core plugin ships no model at all. It is the agent chat plus a router,

, which other plugins (code suggestions, speech to text, vector search) also use. Backends are separate plugins that register on activation: on-device GGUF models through llama.cpp, Gemini, and an OpenAI-compatible backend. Three details mattered more than the diagram:

items.s: Load order is not guaranteed.
Plugins load in parallel, so each backend registers through a lifecycle listener on AI Core and re-registers whenever it comes back.
Class loaders are a hard boundary.
Each plugin has its own, so only plain JDK types cross it. For the same reason the network code uses
HttpURLConnection
instead of OkHttp, which would collide with the host IDE's older copy, and the MCP client is written by hand because the official Kotlin SDK had no Android target.
Optional behaviour is a type, not a flag.
A backend that doesn't implement
HistoryCapableBackend
silently gets single-turn calls: a plausible reply, no error, and the conversation gone. So the test asserts the declaration instead of trusting behaviour to catch it.

body.text: Size the model to the RAM that is actually free

runs.s: On a phone, free RAM changes every time the user switches apps, and the KV cache is the largest allocation a model load makes. The local backend used to create every context at a fixed 4,096 tokens. I replaced that with a policy that reads the model's GGUF header and the device's free memory at load time (

items.s: A q8_0 KV cache with flash attention.

That's 34 bytes per 32 elements, a little over half of f16. llama.cpp refuses it when the model's head width doesn't divide into 32-element blocks, so the load falls back to f16 at a context sized for f16, and a device test runs that fallback on an arm64 phone. I tested the quantized cache with Llama 3.2 1B on a device with 3 GB of RAM or less and a prompt of about 10K tokens, which the log prefills in six slices.
Sliced prefill.
Once
n_ctx
could exceed the batch's fixed capacity, a long prompt could overrun the batch and corrupt the heap, so the prompt is now decoded in slices.

runs.s: Before a model loads, a pre-flight check compares its estimated footprint with free RAM and warns
(expect a quick, hard failure). It never refuses: Cancel is the default, "Proceed anyway" is there for the user about to close other apps, and if a reading fails, it fails open.
Demo: the pre-flight dialog warning that a 13B model needs about 7.3 GB to load plus 3.4 GB to run on a device with 6.3 GB free (
Models picked through the Storage Access Framework used to be copied into the app sandbox, gigabytes at a time. Now the backend keeps the persisted URI and hands llama.cpp a
path so it can mmap the file in place, and a watcher unloads the model if the file goes away. The native library ships for arm64-v8a only, and the build fails if another ABI ends up in the package.

Early on, if the selected local backend wasn't ready, a request could quietly go to another installed backend. That looks like resilience, but for someone who chose an on-device model so their code stays on the phone, it's a privacy bug that also spends their API quota. The router now resolves the backend strictly from the stored selection: installed, missing or none. If it isn't ready, the request stops, the message says that nothing was sent, and each case gets its own fix.

The local backend declares no INTERNET permission, so Android itself enforces that prompts and code stay on the device. The MCP plugin asks only for network access, with no file or project permissions. The cloud backends tag their sockets with
, so inference traffic is visible on its own.

body.text: Tool calls a small model can't get wrong

runs.s: A cloud model and a 1B model on a phone need different strategies. For Gemini and OpenAI I moved from a text envelope to native function calling. With text, models produced payloads with unescaped quotes or newlines, and calls that looked valid were skipped without an error. The extractor now reports malformed or truncated replies instead of letting the loop claim success, and a small parser catches Gemini's undocumented
The local model keeps the text protocol, but its output is constrained by a

, and the tool name must be one of the registered tools. The trap is that the grammar is derived from the tool list. When another plugin adds tools, rebuilding the router alone leaves a token mask that forbids every new tool. The build is green and the only symptom is "the model ignores the tools". So the router, executor, grammar and the prompt's tool list are rebuilt together behind one
reference, and a run in flight keeps the snapshot it started with.
Context is the other budget. A tool result gets 4,000 characters by default, sized for a 4,096-token local context.

pages by start and end line instead of cutting mid-line. Tools contributed by other plugins are capped at 12 in the prompt, with 200 characters of description each, because one MCP server can advertise ninety. When a chat passes 80% of the backend's context window, older turns are summarized; the on-device backend cuts the history instead.

body.text: Feed the agent evidence, and gate what it touches

runs.s: The most useful fix had nothing to do with the model.
used to report success before the build had run, so the agent never learned that its code was broken. Now it waits for the build callback, up to ten minutes, and
takes an 8,000-character window from the first compiler error, not the log's tail, which was mostly Gradle's closing summary.

A progress guard cuts loops. Three turns with no tool batch the run hasn't already tried stops it as cycling, and re-issuing a batch that just succeeded counts as done. Every tool that changes the project or starts a build needs approval, and that comes from the handler's own

; I removed the name-based list that could bypass it. Tools from other plugins run outside the path containment that covers the built-in handlers, so they always ask, never offer "Always allow", and the dialog flattens and caps their name, description and source label. Otherwise a remote server could forge the dialog's structure with a newline.

Testing follows the same idea. The memory gate, context policy and load diagnostics have no Android dependency, so every boundary runs as a JVM unit test; what only a device can prove, like the f16 fallback and 16 KB page alignment, has a device test. The prebuilt llama.cpp AAR carries a SHA-256 of its C++ source, and a test checks it, so a stale native library can't ship quietly.

items.s: Start with the plugin boundary.

Moving the agent out of the app almost a year in meant migrating every setting from each place it had lived, once, without overwriting a value the user had changed since. A boundary on day one avoids that.
Budget the built-in tools for small models from the start.

I capped contributed tools but not the built-ins. A teammate later measured the local model's opening prompt at about 1,780 tokens, over half of it the tool list, read at about 12 tokens a second on a Pixel 6 Pro, and gave small models a compact allowlist of ten tools.
Measure on the cheapest target phone earlier, and write the numbers down.
The number that matters is generation speed on the weakest device you plan to support, and I should have been tracking it from the first week, not the last.
